passage: Yogesh reached the temple hall early for the Sunday meal, and the smell of the big kitchen pulled him back to being ten years old, sitting cross-legged beside his grandfather. Aunties called his name and teased him about his beard. Today he had brought a colleague, Dhruv, who followed no faith and stood stiffly by the shoe rack. "Nobody will quiz you," Yogesh said. "Just eat." Soon Dhruv was drying steel plates beside an old man who asked about his work and never about his beliefs. At the door the old man said, "Come again, whenever you like." Dhruv laughed, a little surprised at himself.

qa.q: Who did Yogesh bring to the Sunday meal?
qa.a: Yogesh brought a colleague, Dhruv, who followed no faith.

qa.q: Why might the temple hall matter so much to Yogesh, and what does the smell do for him?
qa.a: It gives him a warm sense of belonging among people who know him, and the kitchen smell brings back fond memories of childhood with his grandfather.

qa.q: How could Yogesh keep the welcome easy for Dhruv in the weeks ahead?
qa.a: Invite him without pressure, never ask him to take part in anything he doesn't want to, and let him decide whether to return.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt at the shoe rack, and why did that change?
qa.a: He probably felt like an outsider and stiff with nerves, but relaxed when he was given a plain task and met with curiosity about his work instead of questions about belief.

grounding: Shows a young man finding meaning and belonging in his faith community while warmly including someone outside it.

passage:
Dear Payal,

Toronto was lonely for the first two months. Work, microwave dinners, video calls with Mummy at odd hours. You know how I get.

Then, one Sunday, I walked into the gurdwara near my flat. An uncle handed me a head covering and pointed me to the langar hall. By evening I was rolling rotis with five aunties who laughed at my lopsided rotis and fed me twice. Now I do seva every weekend. It feels like home.

Last month I brought my colleague Mei, who had never been inside a gurdwara. Some people stared, but one aunty sat her down and explained everything, patiently. Mei came back the next week on her own.

That's what I love most. The door is open, and the food is for anyone who walks in.

Come visit and I'll put you to work in the kitchen.

Baljeet

qa.q: What did the uncle hand Baljeet on the first Sunday?
qa.a: The uncle handed Baljeet a head covering.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel in Toronto before finding the gurdwara?
qa.a: Baljeet felt lonely, with only work, microwave dinners and video calls.

qa.q: What makes this community a healthy place to belong?
qa.a: It gives Baljeet meaning and support through seva, while staying open and welcoming to outsiders like Mei.

qa.q: How might Mei have felt on her first visit?
qa.a: Mei might have felt nervous when some people stared, then welcomed and at ease when an aunty explained everything, enough to return alone.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding meaning and belonging in a faith community while it stays open to people outside it.

passage:
So the podcast wants the story of the Ganpati pandal? Okay. I'm Indu, I'm on the committee in our Nagpur colony, and this happened last year.

The committee is like family. Ten days of aarti, cooking together, kids running around. When my father was in hospital, these people brought food for a month. That's what belonging feels like.

Last year Tejas, who's just moved in and says he doesn't believe in God, offered to help with the lights. One member said, "Only people who do the pooja should be on the committee."

I stood up in the meeting, heart racing. "The pandal is for the whole colony. Tejas can do the lights, and he doesn't have to pray. Everyone eats the prasad."

People argued a bit. Then they said yes. Tejas stayed up till two wiring the lights, and on the last night he danced at the visarjan with everyone.

qa.q: What did Tejas offer to help with?
qa.a: Tejas offered to help with the lights.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when standing up in the meeting?
qa.a: Indu felt nervous, with a racing heart, but also determined to keep the pandal open to everyone.

qa.q: How did Indu balance belonging with openness?
qa.a: Indu valued the committee's support like family, while arguing that people outside the faith could also join and help.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when he heard the member's comment?
qa.a: Tejas might have felt unwelcome and unsure whether to stay, before being included and joining the celebration.

grounding: Shows a young adult who finds meaning in a faith community and speaks up to keep it open to someone outside it.
